samvardhana motherson international limited '(Q1Motherson has again
outperformed industry growth. What were the 
key drivers of this outperformance?
FY26 has been another year that demonstrates the resilience and structural advantages built into Motherson’s business model. Our revenue for the year grew 11% year-on-year, even as the broader automotive industry in developed economies remained relatively subdued. This outperformance is no accident – it is the result of deliberate, multi-year choices about how we structure the business.
At the heart of this is our 3CX10 strategy: no single country to contribute more than 10% of revenue, no single customer more than 10%, and no single component more than 10%. This diversi/f_ication is our most important buﬀer against any regional or sectoral slowdown. When passenger vehicle demand in Europe or North America softens, our growth engines in India, ASEAN, and other emerging markets continue to /f_ire. Emerging economies contributed meaningfully to our outperformance in FY26, with strong LV and CV volumes in these geographies more than oﬀsetting softness in developed markets.
We are also powertrain-agnostic. Whether 
OEMs move faster or slower toward electri/f_ication, we supply across ICE, hybrid, and EV platforms. This posture has been an important diﬀerentiator in a year when several large OEMs recalibrated their EV timelines. Our booked business as of FY26 stood at USD 96.0 billion, re/f_lecting customer trust across powertrain types.
Increasing content per vehicle has been 
another key driver. As vehicles become more complex – whether through advanced driver assistance systems, electri/f_ication of auxiliary systems, or premium interiors – Motherson’s wallet share per unit increases even when overall volumes are /f_lat. Over and above this, inorganic growth through disciplined Q&Aacquisitions has added capabilities and geographies that organic growth alone could not have delivered as quickly.
Additionally, a key pillar of our 
outperformance strategy has been scaling up businesses beyond automotive by leveraging our core D.E.M.A.L. capabilities – Design, Engineering, Manufacturing, Assembly, and Logistics. Over the years, we have consciously built these capabilities not for a single industry, but as a broader manufacturing and integration platform that can be extended across sectors. This approach has enabled us to successfully enter and scale newer businesses such as aerospace, consumer electronics, logistics and technology, among others. As these businesses continue to grow, they provide an additional layer of diversi/f_ication and reduce dependence on the underlying growth rate of the global automotive industry. Importantly, many of these sectors are currently in a high-growth phase, allowing Motherson to participate in new opportunity pools while leveraging the operational and engineering strengths built over decades.

leverage is at an all-time low. How do you view leverage going forward?
We improved our net leverage ratio to 0.8x Net Debt to EBITDA in FY26 – an all-time low – even as we executed the highest capex in our history and completed multiple acquisitions. This is not a coincidence; it re/f_lects a /f_inancial philosophy that has been consistently applied over many years.

The improvement in leverage, despite active

Our business generates healthy operating cash /f_lows, and these are the primary fuel for our investment activity. Second, capex e/f_f.shorticiency. As mentioned, we 
only invest when we have /f_irm customer orders. This discipline shortens the time between spend and revenue, so capital does not sit idle for long. Our 13 active growth capex projects across emerging markets are all tied to speci/f_ic customer commitments with de/f_ined ramp-up schedules.
Third, acquisition quality. We are disciplined 
about valuations. We do not pursue scale for its own sake.

Q5Passenger vehicle market growth in developed 
economies continued to face headwinds. How do you see these markets evolving, and what impact will they have on Motherson?
The slowdown in developed market passenger vehicle volumes has been real and has had a visible impact on our growth rate in those geographies. The EV transition in Europe and North America did not play out as originally planned by OEMs – consumer adoption was slower than forecast, regulatory timelines shifted, and many large OEMs scaled back or deferred signi/f_icant portions of their EV investment programmes. This recalibration created uncertainty in the supply chain, including for Motherson.
However, this story is beginning to turn. 
During FY26, most major European OEMs restructured their investment programmes and are now aligned with more realistic timelines for the powertrain transition. Critically, the FY27 model launch pipeline from these OEMs is among the largest in years – for some, a record. New model launches are consistently our biggest growth trigger, as fresh platforms come with higher content requirements and often bring us new business wins. Motherson has a meaningful share of business across several of these upcoming platforms, which positions us well for FY27 and beyond.
Also, our exposure has become signi/f_icantly 
more balanced than it was a few years ago. The deliberate diversi/f_ication we have pursued – into emerging markets, into Chinese OEMs that are rapidly expanding their global exports, into non-automotive businesses – means that a soft year in Europe or North America no longer creates a disproportionate drag on our consolidated performance. India and ASEAN delivered strong growth in FY26. Our Consumer Electronics and Aerospace businesses are growing at rates that far exceed the automotive cycle.
Looking ahead, global LV production is 
expected to grow from approximately 92 million units in FY26 to around 93 million units in FY27. Combined with the launch pipeline, the improving macro picture in Europe, and our own share gains, we are optimistic about our growth trajectory going into FY27.
Q6Commodity volatility and geo-political uncertainty have 
been persistent themes. How is Motherson navigating these risks?
Commodity costs and geo-political risks are perhaps the most consistent operational challenges in our industry, and FY26 has been no diﬀerent. Copper prices rose by ~38% over FY25, a trend directly relevant to our wiring harness business. Resin prices, which aﬀect our Modules & Polymer Products division, have been in/f_luenced by crude oil price movements linked to developments in the Middle East. The Group has pass-through arrangements with its major customers for raw material price variations, which are actualised periodically. These arrangements are not instantaneous – there can be a settlement lag of one to two quarters – but they provide structural protection over the medium-term.
We also have a dedicated Global Sourcing 
and Procurement team which enables us to leverage our purchasing volumes across geographies to negotiate better terms, build deeper supplier relationships, and reduce exposure to spot market volatility.Q&Achapter 4

Regarding geopolitical disruptions to supply 
chains, our long-standing ‘globally local’ strategy remains our most important hedge. We manufacture in or near the markets we serve. When the United States imposed tariﬀs on imports from certain countries, our locally present facilities were unaﬀected. The Middle East crisis and associated disruptions to Red Sea shipping have had minimal to no impact on our operations because our supply chains are already structured to be geographically resilient. For customer-nominated components, we have back-to-back arrangements with suppliers to pass through any additional costs.
The Morocco and UAE facilities we are 
establishing are also a deliberate response to the evolving trade environment. These locations oﬀer proximity to European customers, favourable trade agreements, and cost structures that enable us to serve developed-market OEMs competitively even as global trade patterns continue to shift.Q7India has signed several FTAs recently. What

India’s trade agreement activity in the past year has been signi/f_icant, and the implications for the automotive sector – and for Motherson speci/f_ically – are genuinely positive, even if some of the bene/f_its will materialise over a multi-year horizon.
The India–EU FTA, concluded in January 2026, 
is the most consequential of these agreements given the concentration of global OEMs in Europe. For the automotive sector, the headline provision is the phased reduction of duties on European cars from 110% to 10%. Even duties on automotive components will be fully phased out over /f_ive to ten years.
The India–EU FTA will bene/f_it Motherson in 
many ways. First, our European OEM customers – who are the largest component of our client base – stand to bene/f_it from expanded Indian market access, which should support their India investment plans and increase volumes for our Indian operations. Second, the zero-duty access for Indian auto components into EU markets enhances the export competitiveness of our Indian manufacturing base, which supplies globally. Third, as European OEMs deepen their manufacturing presence in India in response to the FTA, Motherson, as a locally Q&A

Consumer Electronics has been a standout story in FY26. It is a true re/f_lection of Motherson’s D.E.M.A.L. capabilities – built over decades in complex, high-precision, high-volume automotive production – which is now translating powerfully to other sectors.
Revenue in the Consumer Electronics 
business grew approximately 7.5x year-on-year during FY26, re/f_lecting the step-change nature of bringing new manufacturing facilities online. This kind of sequential acceleration is exactly what we expected when we committed to this business, and it is gratifying to see it manifest in the numbers.
Perhaps the most important milestone of the

For a business that has been investing heavily in capacity, this re/f_lects both the quality of the execution and the scale of volumes being processed. Our targeted annual production run-rate of 14 to 16 million units, from the /f_irst two facilities, was achieved in Q4FY26 – right on schedule.
Looking ahead, the third facility is on track for commissioning in Q3FY27 and will include added upstream integration capabilities. This will both increase our production capacity and improve our cost structure by bringing more of the value chain in-house. The Consumer Electronics business is on a clear path from scale-up to a mature, self-sustaining contributor to group pro/f_itability, and we are excited about its trajectory.chapter 4

'/ annual report  (&(+#(&(,Q9Aerospace has 
grown rapidly and is increasingly being 
seen as a strategic growth vertical. What is the long-term vision?
Aerospace is another clear demonstration of how Motherson’s strategy of leveraging its core engineering and manufacturing capabilities into adjacent high-growth sectors can create signi/f_icant value. Three years ago, this was a nascent business. Today, it is a meaningful contributor with a clearly de/f_ined growth runway.
In FY26, the Aerospace business delivered

The order book grew 20%+ year-on-year to USD 1.6 billion, providing strong multi-year revenue visibility. This is signi/f_icant – aerospace contracts are long-duration by nature, which means this order book translates into a predictable and growing revenue stream over the next several years.
During the year, we expanded our product 
portfolio across multiple platforms. We secured orders for metallic parts, sub-assemblies and wiring harnesses in business jets and rotary-wing aircraft, adding to our existing capabilities in /f_ixed-wing commercial platforms. This diversi/f_ication across segments – commercial aviation and business aviation – mirrors the multi-customer and multi-segment strategy that has served us well in automotive, and for similar reasons: it reduces concentration risk and opens multiple avenues for growth.
What makes Motherson well-suited to

We are deepening our engagement with existing customers and actively pursuing new programme wins, which should continue to expand both our content and our customer base.

The combination of a growing global /f_leet and the shift toward lighter and more electronically complex aircraft – all of which increases the complexity and value of the systems we supply – makes this a compelling long-term opportunity for us.
Q10How would you describe Motherson’s 
progress in sustainability over the past year?
During FY26, we have further strengthened the integration of sustainability across our operations and long-term planning, focusing on the topics that are most materially important to all stakeholders, such as climate transition, water preservation, waste management, and employee engagement. As we continue to grow and evolve, we remain focused on building an organisation that delivers enduring value through responsible leadership, value creation, and building trust. This year has seen continued progress across a broad spectrum of topics within our three pillars of Sustainability: Planet, People and Governance. For example, we have made signi/f_icant progress with our renewable energy strategy through both increased sourcing and the scaling up of our own solutions. We conducted a group-wide employee engagement survey that reached all our permanent employees globally, as important stakeholders in Motherson, with the learning and insights gained guiding our actions. We are leveraging our internal capabilities through Motherson Technology Solutions to develop systems and tools that harmonise our global business and create value.

India continues to distinguish itself as one of the fastest-growing 
major economies globally, supported by strong domestic fundamentals and a stable macroeconomic framework. According to projections from the International Monetary Fund, India’s economy is expected to expand by around 6.5%, while the Reserve Bank of India projects a slightly higher real GDP growth of 6.6% in FY27, moderating from 7.7% in FY26, as outlined in its latest monetary policy communication.

US Trade Tariﬀs: A structural realignment of

The single most consequential development for the global

Beginning 03 April 2025, a 25% tariﬀ took eﬀect on imported automobiles and a broad set of automotive parts – including engines, transmissions, powertrain components, and electrical systems. A separate 25% tariﬀ on steel and aluminium imports also came into force. A baseline tariﬀ of 10% on goods from all countries, with higher reciprocal levies on select markets, added further layering to the cost environment. The tariﬀ regime was subsequently extended in October 2025 to cover medium and heavy-duty vehicles (25%) and buses (10%), with USMCA-compliant imports receiving partial or conditional relief. An import adjustment oﬀset of 3.75% of aggregate vehicle MSRP was made available to US-assembling OEMs for a transitional period, declining to 2.5% from May 2026.
The /f.shortinancial toll on the global automotive industry has been 
signi/f.shorticant. OEMs globally have collectively absorbed billions of dollars in tariﬀ-related costs, with several announcing meaningful earnings downgrades. The tariﬀ structure has also introduced the concept of ‘stacking’ – where components crossing multiple borders accumulate cumulative duty exposure – increasing complexity in cost modelling and customer pricing negotiations. The supply chain environment has deteriorated meaningfully in 
the second half of FY26, after a period of relative stabilisation earlier in the year. The most acute new disruption has come from the Iran con/f.shortlict, which has closed or substantially restricted access to the Strait of Hormuz – a critical node in global maritime trade through which signi/f.shorticant volumes of automotive parts, raw materials, and /f.shortinished vehicles transit. Shipping insurers have increased premiums on Gulf routes, logistics companies are rerouting cargo, and freight costs on aﬀected lanes have risen sharply. For the automotive supply chain, which relies heavily on just-in-time delivery, extended transit times and route uncertainty add meaningful inventory and cost risk.
Earlier in the year, the tariﬀ environment introduced a diﬀerent 
form of supply chain stress: the risk of ‘tariﬀ stacking’ on crossborder component /f.shortlows, pressure on USMCA compliance and content documentation, and a strategic impetus among OEMs to accelerate US manufacturing localisation. These dynamics have prompted a structural rethink of global network design, with resilience and robustness increasingly displacing pure cost optimisation as the primary criterion. Alongside these macro disruptions, a second-order semiconductor tightness also emerged in 2025, arising from a trade standoﬀ aﬀecting Netherlands-based chipmakers – a reminder that electronics supply chains remain structurally fragile. In our own operations, we have continued to strengthen supplier diversi/f.shortication, build inventory buﬀers for critical materials, and deploy multi-modal logistics solutions. The con/f.shortlict in Iran reinforces our commitment to maintaining supply continuity for our customers as an absolute operational priority.
OEM industry stress and supplier landscape
The /f.shortinancial health of the global automotive industry has diverged sharply between OEMs and suppliers in FY26. OEMs have borne the brunt of stagnant volumes, elevated input costs, tariﬀ exposure, and the capital demands of the electri/f.shortication transition, with a considerable decline in their EBITDA margins. This compression has led to OEM production adjustments, model launch deferrals, and intensi/f.shortied pressure on supplier pricing. Automotive supplier distress metrics have, however, shown some improvement, with the share of suppliers in /f.shortinancial distress declining from approximately 31% in CY 2024 to approximately 24% in CY 2025, supported by eﬀective cost management and pricing discipline. M&A activity in the supplier sector has rebounded after historic lows in CY 2024, with deal volume increasing – particularly in the powertrain and electronics segments – as companies seek scale, technology alignment, and portfolio rationalisation. For us, this environment requires heightened customer engagement, transparent cost discussions, and a focus on the product categories where our value proposition is most diﬀerentiated.
Climate policy and ESG mandates
Sustainability regulation and ESG disclosure requirements continued to gain ground in FY26, though the pace and certainty of regulatory transition have become more geographically uneven. In the EU, the broader political debate around the achievability of 2035 ICE phase-out timelines is prompting recalibration, with the automotive package discussion centring on a more technology-inclusive path to decarbonisation. Despite this, mandatory ESG disclosure requirements under frameworks such as CSRD are expanding the scope of sustainability reporting across the value chain, including for suppliers. The Iran con/f.shortlict, paradoxically, may accelerate the momentum toward electri/f.shortication in some markets as consumers and policymakers respond to energy price volatility. In India, the government’s PLI scheme, green manufacturing incentives, and EV ecosystem investment are reshaping procurement strategies and in/f.shortluencing OEM sourcing decisions. Global light vehicle development
Fiscal year 2026 marked a period of strategic recalibration for global automotive OEMs as they adapted to evolving demand patterns and an increasingly complex operating environment. A key theme during the year was the reassessment of electri/f.shortication strategies, as the pace of electric vehicle adoption varied signi/f.shorticantly across regions. While China continued to witness strong growth in electric vehicle penetration, supported by a well-developed ecosystem and cost competitiveness, markets such as Europe and North America experienced a moderation in growth momentum due to aﬀordability challenges, infrastructure constraints, and evolving policy support. This divergence prompted OEMs to adopt a more balanced and region-speci/f.shortic approach to powertrain strategies, with an increasing emphasis on hybrid technologies alongside battery-electric vehicles.
At the same time, consumer demand remained selective and increasingly price sensitive. While premiumisation trends continued, particularly in the form of higher demand for SUVs and feature-rich vehicles, entry-level segments faced pressure in several developed markets due to aﬀordability constraints.Supply-side conditions improved signi/f.shorticantly during the year, with semiconductor availability normalising and logistics disruptions easing. A de/f.shortining trend during the year has been the

This has led to a more pragmatic, phased approach, with OEMs increasingly prioritising hybrid powertrains and /f.shortlexible platforms that support multiple propulsion technologies. Rider Dome:

The acquisition will enable Motherson Elastomers, Australia (including industrial products from Motherson Elastomers, India), to accelerate its market penetration by giving direct access to an already established customer base.

Adani (Dighi Port):
In December 2025, SAMIL, through its logistics joint venture Samvardhana Motherson Hamakyorex Engineered Logistics Limited (SAMRX), entered into an agreement with Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Limited to develop an automotive-focused export terminal at Dighi Port, Maharashtra in India.

The Integrated Assemblies division provides end-to-
end integrated module solutions for the automotive industry, specialising in assembly, logistics, testing, and engineering services. The division’s portfolio includes safety-critical and complex vehicle modules such as cockpit systems, centre consoles, door panels, headliners, front-end assemblies, and other interior and structural modules.
Built around customer proximity, 
just-in-sequence (JIS) delivery, and compatibility with modular vehicle architectures, the division operates as a Tier-0.5 
partner, extending beyond traditional Tier-1 responsibilities. By working closely with OEMs to manage the manufacturing, sequencing, and integration of major vehicle modules into the assembly process, the division improves production ef/f.shorticiency, reduces complexity, and enables /f.shortlexible programme execution across global platforms.

Aerospace .
The Aerospace division is advancing rapidly toward becoming a 
comprehensive manufacturing and solutions partner for global aerospace original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). It is one of the fastest-growing divisions for Motherson. The division delivers a wide range of aerospace-grade products and services spanning metallics, composites, wiring harnesses, and thermoplastics, supported by strong capabilities in machining, sheet-metal fabrication, surface treatments, and complex assemblies, catering to both /f.shortixed-wing and rotary-wing platforms.
TThe Aerospace division’s capabilities have 
been developed through a phased approach, supported by strategic acquisitions and organic expansion. The acquisition of CIM Tools in FY22 and AD 
Industries in FY25 has strengthened core capabilities across machining, structural components, sheet metal fabrication, composites, and hydraulic assemblies, while the integration of SMAST (India) has enhanced its presence in Electrical Wiring and Interconnect Systems (EWIS). 
Together, these capabilities form a complementary 
portfolio with limited overlap, enabling the division to expand its addressable scope and offer integrated solutions to global aerospace OEMs. 
Aerospace division’s portfolio today covers the full 
aircraft, business and commercial, from cockpit to tail, supporting structures and systems for the fuselage, wings, engines, landing gear, doors, cabins, The division is evolving 
into a comprehensive manufacturing and solutions partner for global OEMs, spanning the full aircraft—from cockpit to tail.

Preamble
Motherson is a people-centric global organization operating across 47 countries with approximately 207,366 employees. The Company is committed to upholding human rights, dignity, equality, inclusion, and diversity through various Board-approved policies. We foster an inclusive and collaborative culture that values the contributions and potential of every employee.
Respect for human rights is integral to our values and operations. 
We are committed to upholding internationally recognised human rights standards, ensuring fair treatment, dignity, and respect for all employees, contractors, and stakeholders. 
Building a Strong Workforce
Motherson globally employed approximately 199,593 and 207,366 employees as of March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026, respectively.
Diversity & Inclusion
Motherson promotes a diverse, inclusive, and respectful workplace free from discrimination, harassment, and intimidation. The Company follows a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour and fosters a culture of trust, respect, and collaboration under its “One Motherson” philosophy i.e. TO BE A GLOBALLY PREFERRED SUSTAINABLE SOLUTIONS PROVIDER for our customers.
The increase in workforce during the year was primarily driven by 
inorganic growth arising from strategic acquisitions and business combinations. The integration of acquired entities expanded the Company’s global footprint and operational capabilities, resulting in the addition of employees across multiple geographies and business segments. This growth has strengthened the Company’s talent pool, enhanced domain expertise, and supported the execution of its long-term growth strategy.
Employee Well-being
Employee safety, well-being, engagement, and work-life balance remain key priorities. The Company leverages technology-enabled communication platforms, /f.shortlexible working arrangements, and modern workplaces to enhance employee experience, collaboration, and productivity.
Employee communication and engagement remained at the 
heart of our approach and are facilitated by technology. To foster a more connected organization, the Company has been using various tools to stay connected with the workforce, providing emotional support.At Motherson, we have pritiorized our employee’s safety, wellbeing, and work /f.shortlexibility. This has not only enabled us to be more responsive to customer demands, more resilient to disruption and more productive in our work, but also attains approach towards work life balance, by providing /f.shortlexible working hours and also introduction of /f.shortive days working in various organizations. Today, our o/f_f.shortices have integrated technology into their designs to deliver an experience far beyond the traditional way of working. Our objective is to create and sustain social asset by enhancing coordination, collaboration and communication at workplace. Our aim is to provide an environment that fosters workplace happiness and promotes employee well-being.
During the year, the Company conducted multiple Annual Health 
check-ups, /f.shortitness sessions, wellness programmes across various units/operations of Chairman O/f_f.shortice South Asia.
Learning and Development
Motherson is committed to fostering a culture of continuous learning, capability building, and professional growth through structured training programmes, leadership development initiatives, mentorship opportunities, and digital learning platforms. Guided by the “BY-BY (By Yourself, Better Yourself)”
philosophy, employees are encouraged to take ownership of their personal and professional development.
Quality Circles remain a key pillar of employee engagement and 
innovation, promoting collaborative problem-solving and continuous improvement. As of December 2025, 2,167 active Quality Circles had successfully completed 6,039 projects, re/f.shortlecting the strong participation of employees in driving operational excellence and innovation.
The Company also maintains a robust skill-mapping framework to 
monitor workforce capabilities and align individual career aspirations with organisational objectives. This approach supports employee development, enhances engagement and retention, and helps employees build meaningful and ful/f.shortilling careers within the organisation.
Continuous learning and capability development remain integral 
to Motherson’s people strategy. During FY 2025-26, the Company further strengthened its learning ecosystem through a combination of technical, functional, leadership, and behavioural development programmes. Employees were provided access to structured training interventions, digital learning platforms, and knowledge-sharing initiatives aimed at enhancing professional Human Resources

Opportunity to grow
Motherson believes in providing Equal Growth Opportunities to all those who have the ability and willingness to perform. Meritocracy is the only criteria to rise in rank. Employee Retention and Long-Term Value Creation
Motherson recognizes that its employees are integral to the Company’s sustained growth and success. In line with its commitment to attracting, retaining, and motivating high-performing talent, the Company has implemented the Motherson 
Employee Stock Option Scheme, 2025 (Motherson ESOP Scheme 2025). The scheme aims to foster a stronger sense of ownership among employees by aligning their interests with the long-term objectives and performance of the Company.
The ESOP Scheme serves as a key component of the Company’s 
employee retention strategy by rewarding employees for their contribution to the Company’s growth and enabling them to participate in the value created for shareholders. Through this initiative, Motherson seeks to strengthen employee engagement, enhance retention of critical talent, encourage long-term commitment, and reinforce a culture of performance, accountability, and shared success.Combined with the Company’s focus on continuous learning, career development, merit-based progression, and employee well-being, the Motherson ESOP Scheme 2025 further supports the Company’s objective of building a motivated, future-ready, and high-performing workforce capable of delivering sustainable growth.
Recognition & Rewards Framework
Motherson’s recognition and rewards framework is designed to acknowledge individual and team contributions that drive business performance, innovation, customer satisfaction, and adherence to the Company’s values. The framework combines performance-linked rewards, long-service awards, career development opportunities, and structured recognition programmes to foster a culture of excellence, accountability, and continuous improvement. Through timely and meaningful recognition, the Company seeks to enhance employee engagement, motivation, and retention across its global operations.
Open Door Communication to Create Trust & Transparency
Motherson fosters a culture of trust, transparency, and open communication through its Open-Door Policy, Whistle Blower Policy, and other employee-centric policies. Multiple engagement platforms, including interaction sessions, communication forums, work councils, and cross-functional teams, facilitate two-way dialogue, collaboration, and continuous improvement.
The Company maintains a structured grievance redressal 
mechanism and leverages digital engagement tools to enhance connectivity, knowledge sharing, and employee collaboration. Regular employee engagement surveys help assess satisfaction levels and drive workplace improvements based on employee feedback.
These initiatives collectively support a safe, inclusive, and 
engaging work environment, reinforcing Motherson’s commitment to employee well-being and participation.
Health & Safety
Health and safety remain a core priority at Motherson, guided by the principle of “Safety First.” The Company has established robust systems, processes, and training programmes to minimise workplace risks and promote a safe and healthy working environment for all employees.
The Company is committed to preventing occupational hazards, 
fostering a culture where employees can freely raise safety concerns, and continuously strengthening safety practices across its operations. An Occupational Health and Safety Principles Statement, approved by the Board, provides the framework for this commitment.

Environmental Responsibility 
Motherson is committed to minimising the environmental impact of its operations and integrating sustainability into its business practices. The Company complies with applicable environmental regulations, promotes responsible resource management, and continuously works to reduce its environmental footprint across the value chain.
Environmental considerations are embedded throughout the

Motherson continues to advance its sustainability agenda through 
increased adoption of renewable energy, including solar and wind power, and the implementation of energy-e/f_f.shorticient technologies such as LED lighting across its facilities. The Company commissioned its /f.shortirst captive power project in Uttar Pradesh, marking a signi/f.shorticant milestone in its journey towards greater energy e/f_f.shorticiency, renewable energy adoption, and reduction of its carbon footprint.
Aligned with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and global 
climate action initiatives, Motherson remains committed to reducing environmental impacts, promoting sustainable business practices, and contributing to a cleaner and greener future for future generations.
In this respect, Motherson is actively working on following 
Principles to minimize the environmental impact of its current operations and supply chain, focusing on the following areas:
(a) Minimise and wherever possible eliminate the emission of 
greenhouse gases.
(b) Improve energy e/f_f.shorticiency in all areas and maximise access to sources of renewable energy.
(c) Improve water utilisation e/f_f.shorticiency and harvesting.
(d) Minimise and wherever possible eliminate waste focusing on the increased application of recycling solutions.(e) Focus on climate positive actions and maximising economic circularity.
(f) Adapt and maintain compliance to evolving regional and country speci/f.shortic environmental goals.

Risk Management 
The Group has a global presence and decentralised management structure. During the /f.shortinancial year 2025 –26, the Group navigated a complex operating environment marked by persistent internal and external challenges. Macroeconomic uncertainties and geopolitical developments continued to in/f.shortluence the Group’s overall risk landscape throughout the year. At the macro level, the Group is exposed to risks associated with global organisations and the automotive industry in particular. E/uniFB00ectively mitigating risks from all directions is one of the challenges that the Group targets. Risk is an inherent component of business growth and strategic decision making, but not all risks are not equal. Risk mitigation e/uniFB00orts are calibrated according to the likelihood of exposure and the potential downside of an incident. The Group is exposed to various risks within each of its business segments and products. 
Risk Management structure
The /f.shortirst step for risk management is in creating an e/uniFB00ective risk management system is to understand the qualitative distinctions among the types of risks that organisations face. The Board of Directors of a legal entity are responsible for risk oversight under applicable laws The Board of Directors has set up a Risk Management Committee, (“RMC”) to periodically, inter-alia, review Operating Risks, Regulatory Risks, Strategic RisksCyber Security Risks amongst others in the business and their mitigating factors. RMC periodically review the risk(s) and their mitigation strategies for all of its subsidiaries and joint ventures. The risk management and mitigation strategies are governed by a structured, multi-layered oversight mechanism:
• Board of Directors: Holds ultimate oversight and 
responsibility for framing and monitoring the risk management plan, ensuring that risk mitigation is embedded in all aspects of operations and strategy under the framework assessed by the management in the business environment under which it operates. 
• Risk Management Committee (RMC): A dedicated committee at the board level oversees the risk management process. The Committee review on periodic basis risk assessment, evaluation and mitigation steps taken by the management team including the Chief Risk O/f_f.shorticers (CRO) of respective business. 1. Risk Identi/f.shortication
Each business division conducts systematic reviews to 
identify and understand risks across three dimensions:
• Risk identi/f.shortication :raising awareness and building 
capability across all teams to recognise risk indicators early.
• Probability evaluation :assessing the likelihood that an identi/f.shortied risk will materialise within a given timeframe.
• Consequence evaluation :determining the impact and potential /f.shortinancial losses to establish the size and priority of each risk.
2.  Risk Measurement
Risks are evaluated and scored on approved parameters to 
determine their signi/f.shorticance and priority:
• Impact classi/f.shortication : rated as Extreme, Moderate or 
Minor based on e/uniFB00ect on /f.shortinancial performance, credit rating, market share, regulatory prosecution and /f.shortines and and health safety issues to employees and third parties.
• Likelihood classi/f.shortication : assessed as Frequent, Likely or Unlikely based on historical data, expert judgement and forward-looking indicators.• Risk impact matrix : combining impact and likelihood ratings to produce a composite risk score that drives prioritisation decisions.
3.  Risk Examination
Identi/f.shortied and measured risks are examined in depth to 
determine the most e/uniFB00ective response strategy:
• Review of available mitigation options, existing 
controls and gap areas requiring new or enhanced measures.
• Assessment of remediation approaches including risk acceptance, transfer, avoidance or reduction strategies.
• Alignment of proposed responses with business continuity and contingency planning requirements.
4.  Risk Implementation
Selected controls and mitigation actions are formally 
executed with clear ownership and governance:
• Deployment of approved controls and remediation 
measures across relevant business divisions and functions.
• Assignment of named accountability to responsible owners with de/f.shortined timelines and deliverables.
• Integration with business continuity and contingency planning to ensure operational preparedness and protection of personnel and assets.
5.  Risk Monitoring
A continuous monitoring mechanism ensures controls 
remain e/uniFB00ective and risks are managed on an ongoing basis:
• Ongoing tracking of implemented measures against 
de/f.shortined effectiveness criteria and performance indicators.
• Structured reporting of outcomes on a de/f.shortined review cycle to senior management and relevant governance bodies.

3. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling and disposing at the end of life, for (a) Plastics (including packaging) (b) E-waste (c) Hazardous waste and (d) other waste.
End of life recycling for automotive products is typically handled by an established reclamation industry, and occurs many years 
after the product has been placed on the market.
At the point of supply of product to the automotive OEM, the majority of packaging used is designed to be both returnable and 
reusable, with closed loop logistics delivery and return solutions in place. Packaging that is not economical to return, such as that used for products exported outside of India, is designed to be recyclable at its end destination.

Yes, we are committed to advancing sustainable practices across our operations. The plastics operations of the Company are 
registered under EPR with the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) as per their applicability for Plastic Waste Management Rules and E-waste.

b. What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the entity?
At Motherson, we adopt a proactive, systematic, and structured approach to the identi/f.shortication and assessment of work 
related hazards and occupational health and safety risks. A combination of routine and non routine processes is employed to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of potential hazards across operations.
Designated and trained personnel conduct regular safety inspection walks to identify existing and potential workplace 
hazards. These inspections support ongoing monitoring of compliance with safety requirements and enable early identi/f.shortication of emerging risks. Periodic and task based risk assessments are conducted across activities, processes, and operational areas to systematically evaluate hazards and determine appropriate control measures.
Monthly and quarterly audits are undertaken to review hazard identi/f.shortication and risk assessment inputs, evaluate the 
e/uniFB00ectiveness of existing controls, and identify opportunities for improvement. Audit outcomes are reviewed by management as part of the continual improvement process. From an equipment and plant perspective, the Company prioritizes planned and preventive maintenance programs. These programs are designed to minimize risks arising from equipment malfunction, degradation, or failure.
Risk assessments are conducted prior to commencement of work, production start ups, or non routine activities to identify 
speci/f.shortic hazards and ensure appropriate controls are in place before execution.
The Company emphasizes active participation of employees in hazard identi/f.shortication and risk management. Ongoing 
training, awareness programs, and monitoring processes are deployed, with continuous improvement measured through qualitative and quantitative objectives, targets, and action plans aligned with international standards and local requirements.
In the event of an incident, a structured investigation process is followed, including escalation to appropriate management 
levels. Investigations focus on root cause analysis, with corrective and preventive actions implemented to mitigate future risks and prevent recurrence.
Overall, the Company is committed to continuous hazard and risk identi/f.shortication and assessment, supported by employee 
involvement, leadership oversight, and structured improvement mechanisms, thereby promoting a safe and healthy working environment across its operations.

The identity of the Reporting Person is kept con/f.shortidential, and retaliation is strictly prohibited in accordance with the Code of 
Conduct for Employees and Whistleblower Policies. The Company maintains a ‘zero tolerance’ approach towards any form of harassment in the workplace, and every individual is responsible for ensuring their actions and behaviors are free from harassment.

annual report  (&(+#(&(,(-'Executive Summary of Impact Assessment Report
INTRODUCTION
Samvardhana Motherson International Limited ("SAMIL"), through its Water, Sanitation, Hygiene and Education ("WASHE") programme, has undertaken targeted interventions to improve infrastructure, sanitation, and learning environments in government schools located near its manufacturing operations. The programme responds to persistent challenges faced by government schools-particularly in rural and peri-urban areas-where inadequate WASH facilities, poor classroom conditions, and limited access to digital learning tools adversely a/uniFB00ect student comfort, participation, and overall educational experience.
This impact assessment, covers WASHE interventions implemented between the years from 2022 to 2024 across selected government 
schools in Greater Noida (Uttar Pradesh) and Haryana. The assessment examines programme performance using the OECD-DAC evaluation framework. A mixed-methods methodology was adopted, combining quantitative surveys of students and teachers, focus group discussions, and a review of programme documentation.
PROGRAMME COVERAGE AND INTERVENTIONS
The WASHE programme delivered a comprehensive set of interventions structured around three thematic pillars:
Infrastructure and WASH: Renovation and construction of sanitation facilities, provision of water access, installation of rainwater 
harvesting systems, Kota stone /f.shortlooring in classrooms and corridors, roof maintenance and waterproo/f.shorting, whitewashing, and related civil works aimed at improving safety, hygiene, and durability of school infrastructure.
Furniture and Learning Environment: Provision of desks and benches to replace /f.shortloor seating, installation of lights and fans to improve 
classroom comfort, and BaLA (Building as Learning Aid) paintings to create engaging, child-friendly spaces.
Digital Education: Installation of smart classrooms equipped with digital boards and supporting hardware, accompanied by a three-
year Annual Maintenance Contract (AMC). In addition to day schools, the programme supported a Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV) Girls' Hostel, where targeted upgrades were undertaken to address sanitation, water management, structural de/f.shorticiencies, and lack of personal storage for resident students.
KEY FINDINGS
Relevance: The programme was found to be highly relevant to the needs of schools. A large majority of teachers and school management indicated that the interventions directly addressed critical infrastructure gaps that had persisted over several years. Students also reported visible improvements in cleanliness, comfort, and classroom conditions. The programme aligns well with national initiatives such as Swachh Vidyalaya and Samagra Shiksha, while also responding to site-speci/f.shortic challenges, including waterlogging in low-lying campuses.
E/uniFB00ectiveness: The WASHE interventions were largely e/uniFB00ective in achieving their intended outputs. Over 90% of teachers reported 
that renovated toilets were fully functional, with water available in or near the facilities. Classroom infrastructure upgrades resulted in improved lighting, ventilation, and seating arrangements. Around two-thirds of teachers reported that student participation in classroom activities improved following the interventions, which they attributed to tangible changes in the learning environment, particularly the shift from /f.shortloor seating to desks and benches, smoother /f.shortlooring and improved ventilation.
Smart classrooms emerged as a key output. At the time of assessment, 80% of teachers reported that smart classrooms were functional 
and being used, while 20% indicated non-functionality primarily due to the expiry of AMC-linked service or subscription packages, rather than equipment failure. In schools where smart classrooms remained operational, 36% of teachers reported daily use, with an additional 24% indicating frequent use.
E/f_f.shorticiency: The programme demonstrated strong time e/f_f.shorticiency, with 96% of respondents indicating that interventions were completed 
within planned timelines. Minor delays were reported in a small number of cases, largely due to external factors such as site-speci/f.shortic constraints and temporary regulatory measures, including restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP). Clear assignment of maintenance responsibilityto schools facilitated orderly handover of assets.
Impact: The assessment identi/f.shorties positive, emerging impacts on school functioning and student experience. Majority of students 
reported that classrooms and facilities were better than before, particularly noting improvements in seating, sanitation, water access and digital learning tools. Qualitative feedback from teachers and school management suggests improved attendance and retention owing to a more conducive classroom environment.
=== page 275 ===
samvardhana motherson international limited(-(In schools where rainwater harvesting systems and walking pathways were constructed, stakeholders reported that chronic 
waterlogging during the monsoon season was resolved, signi/f.shorticantly improving safety and access to classrooms. At the KGBV Girls' Hostel, interventions led to substantial improvements in hygiene, water management, structural safety, and personal storage, enhancing students' dignity, privacy and daily living conditions.
Coherence: The WASHE programme demonstrates strong coherence with the broader education and WASH ecosystem. Qualitative 
evidence indicates that, at the time of programme initiation, most intervention schools had received limited or no prior external infrastructure support and were in a highly deteriorated condition. Any subsequent contributions from other corporates occurred later and did not overlap with WASHE activities. The programme therefore functioned as a gap-/f.shortilling intervention, complementing government e/uniFB00orts rather than duplicating them.
Sustainability: While 96% of respondents expressed con/f.shortidence that improvements are likely to be sustained, the assessment identi/f.shortied 
notable sustainability risks. Schools rely on government maintenance grants typically ranging from INR 50,000 to INR 75,000 per year, which stakeholders reported as insu/f_f.shorticient to cover recurring costs for sanitation facilities, water systems, and digitally enabled infrastructure.Instances of non-functional rainwater harvesting units due to lack of regular maintenance, and smart classrooms becoming inoperative following AMC expiry, highlight constraints within existing government systems for post-installation servicing and renewal.
CONCLUSION
Overall, the assessment concludes that the WASHE programme has been well-targeted, e/uniFB00ectively implemented, and responsive to the foundational infrastructure and learning needs of government schools. By addressing sanitation, physical learning conditions, and access to digital tools in an integrated manner, the programme has contributed to measurable improvements in school environments and student experience. Strengthening government led mechanisms for maintenance /f.shortinancing, service renewal, and addressing remaining infrastructure gaps shall be critical to sustaining and deepening these gains in future phases.
Methodology of the Study
A four-phase structured methodology was adopted for the evaluation of the projects:
Phase Description
1. Consultation & Scoping • Gathering secondary data related to the projects.
• Interviews with SLMTT to understand the details and bene/f.shorticiaries of the project.
2. Research Design • Development of impact maps and primary data collection tools as per the OECD-DAC framework.
3. Data collection, cleaning, and 
analysis• Physical/telephonic interviews with bene/f.shorticiaries.
• Physical/ Online interviews with other relevant stakeholders.
• Analysis of data captured during primary data collection.
• Analysis of qualitative responses to the questionnaires.
4. Reporting • Final Report with key /f.shortindings.
OECD-DAC FrameworkThis study has deployed the OECD-DAC framework evaluation criteria throughout the impact evaluation process to develop a qualitative understanding of the impact created, stakeholder perceptions, and sustenance of the change envisioned under the project.
The OECD DAC Network on Development Evaluation (EvalNet) has de/f.shortined six evaluation criteria – relevance, coherence, e/uniFB00ectiveness, 
e/f_f.shorticiency, impact and sustainability. These criteria are intended to guide evaluations. These have been in use since 1991 and were re/f.shortined in 2019 to improve the quality and usefulness of evaluation and further strengthen the contribution of the evaluation itself to sustainable development.

The Company has adopted a remuneration policy in consonance 
with the industry practices and rewards good performance of the employees of the Company. The policy ensures equality, fairness and consistency in rewarding the employees on the basis of performance against set objectives and the performance of the individuals measured through the annual appraisal process.
Remuneration policy of the Company is designed to create a high- 
performance culture. It enables the Company to attract, retain and motivate employees to achieve results. Our business model promotes customer centricity and requires employee mobility to address project needs.
The Company pays remuneration by way of salary, bene/f.shortits, 
perquisites and allowances to its Executive Director. Annual increments are recommended by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee within the salary scale approved by Members and the Board. Annual increments are e/uniFB00ective April 1 of each year.

DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY
1. Scope and Purpose
1.1 Samvardhana Motherson International Limited (“the 
Company”) equity shares are listed on the BSE Limited 
and the National Stock Exchange of India Limited.
1.2 This Dividend Distribution Policy (“the Policy”) 
de/f.shortines conditions to be considered by the Board for recommending / paying a dividend to the shareholders of the Company. The Board of Directors will recommend any interim / annual dividend based on this Policy, applicable laws, as well as any speci/f.shortic /f.shortinancial or market conditions prevailing at the time.
1.3 Subject to the factors mentioned in para 1.2 above, 
the Company has a consistent dividend policy for “distribution of upto 40% of consolidated pro/f.shortit as dividend and the Board may decide higher dividend in special and exceptional circumstances”.
1.4 The Policy set out the broad criteria to be considered 
for determining the proposed dividend to appropriately reward shareholders through dividends while supporting the future growth of the Company.
2. Dividend Policy
2.1 Dividend Distribution Philosophy.
2.1.1 The Company believes in long term value creation for 
its shareholders while maintaining the desired liquidity 
and leverage ratios and protecting the interest of all the stakeholders. Accordingly, the focus will continue to be on sustainable returns in terms of dividend, in consonance with the dynamics of business environment.
2.2 The circumstances under which shareholders may not 
expect dividend.
2.2.1 The Company shall comply with relevant statutory 
requirements that are applicable to the Company in declaring dividend or retained earnings. Generally, the Board shall determine dividend for a particular period after taking into consideration /f.shortinancial performance of the Company, advice of executive management and other parameters described in the Policy.2.3 The /f.shortinancial parameters that shall be considered while 
declaring dividend.
2.3.1 As in the past, subject to provisions of applicable law, 
the Company’s dividend pay-out will be determined based on available /f.shortinancial resources, investment requirements and taking into account optimal shareholder return.
2.3.2 Based on above and, subject to factors mentioned 
in para 2.4 below, the Company will endeavour to maintain steady level of dividend.
2.4 The internal / external factors that shall be considered 
for declaration of dividend.
2.4.1 When recommending / determining the dividend, the 
company will consider, amongst other matters:
 actual results for the year and the outlook for 
business operations
 providing for anticipated capital expenditures or acquisitions to further enhance shareholder value or meet strategic objectives
 setting aside cash to meet debt repayments
 changes in cost and availability of external /f.shortinancing
 level of dividends paid historically
 retaining earnings to provide for contingencies or unforeseeable events
 the overall economic environment including taxation
 changes in government policy, industry rulings and regulatory provisions
2.5 Policy on utilization of retained earning.
2.5.1 The utilization of retained earnings will include:
 Inorganic / organic growth
=== page 316 ===
annual report  (&(+#(&(,)') Diversi/f.shortication opportunities / capital expenditure
 Fund based requirement of company, its 
subsidiaries, joint ventures and/or other investee companies
 General corporate purposes including contingencies
 Investments in the new/existing business
 Any other permitted use under the Companies Act, 2013 and applicable laws
2.6 Provisions with regard to various classes of shares.
2.6.1 The provisions contained in this policy shall apply to all 
classes of shares of the Company. It may be noted that 
currently the Company has only one class of shares, namely, equity shares.
3. Review and Disclosure
3.1 This policy will be reviewed and amended, as and 
when, required by the Board and/or under applicable laws. Any revisions in the Policy will be communicated to shareholders in a timely manner. The Policy shall be disclosed in the Annual report and on the website of the Company, i.e., ‘www.motherson.com’.4. Limitation
4.1 In the event of any con/f.shortlict between the Act or the 
SEBI Regulations or other statutory enactments (“the Regulations”) and the provisions of this policy, the Regulations shall prevail over this policy. Any subsequent amendment / modi/f.shortication in the Regulations, in this regard, shall automatically apply to this policy.
5. Disclaimer
5.1 The Policy does not constitute a commitment 
regarding future dividends of the Company, but only represents a general guidance regarding payment of dividend.
5.2 The statement of the policy does not in any way 
restrict right of the board to use its discretion in the recommendation of the dividend to be distributed considering various factors mentioned in the policy. Further, subject to the provisions of applicable laws, the board reserves the right to depart from the policy as and when circumstances so warrant.

Annexure 2 To The Independent Auditor’s Report Of Even 
Date On The Standalone Financial Statements Of Samvardhana Motherson International Limited Report on the Internal Financial Controls under Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 of Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”)We have audited the internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to standalone /f.shortinancial statements of Samvardhana Motherson International Limited (“the Company”) as of March 31, 2026 in conjunction with our audit of the standalone /f.shortinancial statements of the Company for the year ended on that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal Financial Controls
The Company’s Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining internal /f.shortinancial controls based on the internal control over /f.shortinancial reporting criteria established by the Company considering the essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”). Auditor’s Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to these standalone /f.shortinancial statements based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) and the Standards on Auditing, as speci/f.shortied under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit of internal /f.shortinancial controls, both issued by ICAI. Those Standards and the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to these standalone /f.shortinancial statements was established and maintained and if such controls operated e/uniFB00ectively in all material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit 
evidence about the adequacy of the internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to these standalone /f.shortinancial statements and their operating e/uniFB00ectiveness. Our audit of internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to standalone /f.shortinancial statements included obtaining an understanding of internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to these standalone /f.shortinancial statements, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating e/uniFB00ectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgement, including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the /f.shortinancial statements, whether due to fraud or error. 
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is su/f_f.shorticient 
and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit opinion on the Company’s internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to these standalone /f.shortinancial statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to 
these Standalone Financial StatementsA company’s internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to standalone /f.shortinancial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of /f.shortinancial reporting and the preparation of /f.shortinancial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal /f.shortinancial controls with reference to standalone /f.shortinancial statements includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly re/f.shortlect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of /f.shortinancial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material e/uniFB00ect on the /f.shortinancial statements.

(i) Amendments to Ind AS 21 - Lack of exchangeability
The Ministry of Corporate A/uniFB00airs (MCA) noti/f.shortied the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules,

assess whether a currency is exchangeable and how it should determine a spot exchange rate when exchangeability is lacking. The amendments also require disclosure of information that enables users of its /f.shortinancial statements to understand how the currency not being exchangeable into the other currency a/uniFB00ects, or is expected to a/uniFB00ect, the entity’s /f.shortinancial performance, /f.shortinancial position and cash /f.shortlows.

(ii) Amendments to Ind AS 1 - Classi/f.shortication of Liabilities as Current or Non-current and Non-current Liabilities with 
Covenants
In August 2025, the MCA noti/f.shortied amendments to paragraphs 69 to 76 of Ind AS 1 to specify the requirements for classifying liabilities as current or non-current. The amendments clarify:
• What is meant by a right to defer settlement
• That a right to defer must exist at the end of the reporting period
• That classi/f.shortication is una/uniFB00ected by the likelihood that an entity will exercise its deferral right
• That only if an embedded derivative in a convertible liability is itself an equity instrument would the terms of a 
liability not impact its classi/f.shortication In addition, a requirement has been introduced to require disclosure when a liability arising from a loan agreement is classi/f.shortied as non-current and the entity’s right to defer settlement is contingent on compliance with future covenants within twelve months.
If there is a breach of a material covenant of a long term loan arrangement on or before the end of the reporting period, resulting in the liability becoming payable on demand as at the reporting date, and the lender agrees—after the reporting period but before the /f.shortinancial statements are approved for issue—not to demand repayment for at least 12 months as a consequence of the breach, this shall be treated as an adjusting event. Accordingly, the entity is not required to classify the liability as current.
The amendments are e/uniFB00ective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025 retrospectively in 
accordance with Ind AS 8.
The amendments have resulted in additional disclosures in Note 17 but have not had an impact on the classi/f.shortication of 
Company’s liabilities.

(c) Foreign currencies
(i) Functional and presentation currency
The Company’s functional currency is Indian Rupee (INR) and the /f.shortinancial statements are presented in Indian Rupee (INR).
(ii) Transactions and balances
Foreign currency transactions are translated into the functional currency using the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions. Foreign exchange gains and losses resulting from the settlement of such transactions and from the translation of monetary assets and liabilities denominated in foreign currencies at year end exchange rates are generally recognised in pro/f.shortit or loss. They are deferred in other comprehensive income if they relate to qualifying cash /f.shortlow hedges
Foreign exchange di/uniFB00erences on foreign currency borrowings are presented in the Statement of pro/f.shortit and loss, within 
/f.shortinance costs. All other foreign exchange gains and losses are presented in the Statement of pro/f.shortit and loss on a net basis within other operating revenue or other expenses.
Non-monetary items that are measured at fair value in a foreign currency are translated using the exchange rates at the 
date when the fair value was determined. Translation di/uniFB00erences on assets and liabilities carried at fair value are reported as part of the fair value gain or loss.
(d) Revenue from contracts with customersRevenue from contracts with customers is recognised when control of the goods or services are transferred to the customer at an amount that re/f.shortlects the consideration to which the Company expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services. The Company has generally concluded that it is the principal in its revenue arrangements, except for the agency services below, because it typically controls the goods or services before transferring them to the customer.
Revenue from sale of components
Revenue from sale of components is recognised at the point in time when control of the asset is transferred to the customer, generally on delivery of the components.
The Company considers whether there are other promises in the contract that are separate performance obligations to 
which a portion of the transaction price needs to be allocated. In determining the transaction price for the sale of components, the Company considers the effects of variable consideration, the existence of signi/f.shorticant /f.shortinancing components, non-cash consideration, and consideration payable to the customer (if any) including price variations.
Variable consideration
If the consideration in a contract includes a variable amount, the Company estimates the amount of consideration to which it will be entitled in exchange for transferring the goods to the customer. The variable consideration is estimated at contract inception and constrained until it is highly probable that a signi/f.shorticant revenue reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognised will not occur when the associated uncertainty with the variable consideration is subsequently resolved.
Volume rebates
The Company applies the most likely amount method or the expected value method to estimate the variable consideration in the contract. The selected method that best predicts the amount of variable consideration is primarily driven by the number of volume thresholds contained in the contract. The most likely amount is used for those contracts with a single volume threshold, while the expected value method is used for those with more than one volume threshold. The Company then applies the requirements on constraining estimates in order to determine the amount of variable consideration that can be included in the transaction price and recognised as revenue. A refund liability is recognised for the expected future rebates (i.e., the amount not included in the transaction price).

Warranty obligations
The Company typically provides warranties for general repairs of defects that existed at the time of sale, as required by law. These assurance-type warranties are accounted for under Ind AS 37 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets.
Revenue from assembly of components
The Company has contracts with customers to assemble, on their behalf, customised components from various parts procured from suppliers identi/f.shortied by the customer. The Company is acting as an agent in these arrangements.
When another party is involved in providing goods or services to its customer, the Company determines whether it is a 
principal or an agent in these transactions by evaluating the nature of its promise to the customer. The Company is a principal and records revenue on a gross basis if it controls the promised goods or services before transferring them to the customer. However, if the Company’s role is only to arrange for another entity to provide the goods or services, then the Company is an agent and will need to record revenue at the net amount that it retains for its agency services.
Revenue from development of tools
The Company develops customised tooling for its customers and recognises its revenue over time using an input method to measure progress towards complete satisfaction of the tool development.
The Company recognises revenue from development of tools over time if it can reasonably measure its progress towards 
complete satisfaction of the performance obligation.
Where the Company cannot reasonably measure the outcome of a performance obligation, but the Company expects to 
recover the costs incurred in satisfying the performance obligation. In those circumstances, the Company recognises revenue only to the extent of the costs incurred until such time that it can reasonably measure the outcome of the performance obligation

Judgments applied in determining amount and timing of revenue
The Company applied the following judgements that signi/f.shorticantly a/uniFB00ect the determination of the amount and timing of revenue from contracts with customers:
(i) Determining the timing of satisfaction of tooling development
The Company concluded that revenue for development of tooling is to be recognised over time because the 
Company’s performance does not create asset with an alternative use to the Company since the tools are customised for each customer and the Company has a legally enforceable right to payment of fair value for performance completed to date.
The Company determined that the input method is the best method in measuring progress of the tooling development 
because there is a direct relationship between the Company’s e/uniFB00ort (i.e., costs incurred) and the transfer of tooling to the customer. The Company recognises revenue on the basis of the total costs incurred relative to the total expected costs to complete the tool.
(ii) Principal versus agent considerations
The Company enters into contracts with its customers to assemble, on their behalf, customised components using various parts procured from suppliers identi/f.shortied by the customer. Under these contracts, the Company provides assembly services (i.e., coordinating the procurement of various parts from the identi/f.shortied suppliers and combining or assembling them into components as desired by the customer). The Company determined that it does not control the goods before they are transferred to customers, and it does not have the ability to direct the use of the component or obtain bene/f.shortits from the component. The following factors indicate that the Company does not control the goods before they are being transferred to customers. Therefore, the Company determined that it is an agent in these contracts.
• The Company is not primarily responsible for ful/f.shortilling the promise to provide the speci/f.shortied equipment.
• The Company does not have inventory risk before or after the speci/f.shortied component has been transferred to the 
customer as it purchases various parts on just-in-time basis and only upon contract of the customer.
• The Company has no discretion in establishing the price for the speci/f.shortied component. The Company’s consideration in these contracts is only based on the di/uniFB00erence between the maximum purchase price quoted by the customer and the cost of various parts purchased from the suppliers.
• In addition, the Company concluded that it transfers control over its services (i.e., assembling the component from various parts), at a point in time, upon receipt by the customer of the component, because this is when the customer bene/f.shortits from the Company’s agency service.
Consultancy IncomeFees earned for the provision of services are recognised over time or point in time as per contract with the customer. In case of contracts where the customer receives and consumes the bene/f.shortits simultaneously, as the services are rendered, the revenue is recognised over the term of the contract.
In cases where the customer receives and consume the services at single point in time, revenue is recognised as and when 
the performance obligation is satis/f.shortied.
Fee and Commission Income
Fees earned for the provision of guarantees are recognised over time as the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the bene/f.shortits, as the services are rendered. The revenue for such contracts is recognised over the term of the guarantee contract.

Trade Receivables
Trade receivables are amounts due from customers for goods sold or services performed in the ordinary course of business. They are generally due for settlement within one year and therefore are all classi/f.shortied as current. Where the settlement is due after one year, they are classi/f.shortied as non-current. Trade receivables are recognised initially at the amount of consideration that is unconditional unless they contain signi/f.shorticant /f.shortinancing components, when they are recognised at fair value. Contract Assets
A contract asset is the entity’s right to consideration in exchange for goods or services that the entity has transferred to the customer. A contract asset is recognised where receipt of consideration is conditional on successful completion of another performance obligation. The impairment of contract assets is measured, presented and disclosed on the same basis as trade receivables. The Company’s contract assets are disclosed in Note 45 as unbilled revenue.
Contract Liabilities
A contract liability is the obligation to transfer goods or services to a customer for which the Company has received consideration (or an amount of consideration is due) from the customer. If a customer pays consideration before the Company transfers goods or services to the customer, a contract liability is recognised when the payment is made or the payment is due (whichever is earlier). Contract liabilities are recognised as revenue when the Company performs under the contract. Contract Liabilities are disclosed in Note 45 as Advances received from customers.
Impairment
An impairment is recognised to the extent that the carrying amount of receivable or asset relating to contracts with customers (a) the remaining amount of consideration that the Company expects to receive in exchange for the goods or services to which such asset relates; less (b) the costs that relate directly to providing those goods or services and that have not been recognised as expenses.

(h) Impairment of non-/f.shortinancial assets
The Company assesses, at each reporting date, whether there is an indication that an asset may be impaired. If any indication exists, or when annual impairment testing for an asset is required, the Company estimates the asset’s recoverable amount. An asset’s recoverable amount is the higher of an asset’s or cash-generating unit’s (CGU) fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use. Recoverable amount is determined for an individual asset, unless the asset does not generate cash in/f.shortlows that are largely independent of those from other assets or groups of assets. When the carrying amount of an asset or CGU exceeds its recoverable amount, the asset is considered impaired and is written down to its recoverable amount.
In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash /f.shortlows are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount rate 
that re/f.shortlects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks speci/f.shortic to the asset. In determining fair value less costs of disposal, recent market transactions are taken into account. If no such transactions can be identi/f.shortied, an appropriate valuation model is used. These calculations are corroborated by valuation multiples, quoted share prices for publicly traded companies or other available fair value indicators.
The Company bases its impairment calculation on detailed budgets and forecast calculations, which are prepared separately 
for each of the Company’s CGUs to which the individual assets are allocated. These budgets and forecast calculations generally cover a period of /f.shortive years. For longer periods, a long-term growth rate is calculated and applied to project future cash /f.shortlows after the /f.shortifth year. To estimate cash /f.shortlow projections beyond periods covered by the most recent budgets/forecasts, the Company extrapolates cash /f.shortlow projections in the budget using a steady or declining growth rate for subsequent years, unless an increasing rate can be justi/f.shortied. In any case, this growth rate does not exceed the long-term average growth rate for the products, industries, or country or countries in which the entity operates, or for the market in which the asset is used. Impairment losses including impairment on inventories, are recognised in the statement of pro/f.shortit and loss
For assets including goodwill, an assessment is made at each reporting date to determine whether there is an indication that 
previously recognised impairment losses no longer exist or have decreased. If such indication exists, the Company estimates the asset’s or CGU’s recoverable amount. A previously recognised impairment loss is reversed only if there has been a change in the assumptions used to determine the asset’s recoverable amount since the last impairment loss was recognised. The reversal is limited so that the carrying amount of the asset does not exceed its recoverable amount, nor exceed the carrying amount that would have been determined, net of depreciation, had no impairment loss been recognised for the asset in prior years. Such reversal is recognised in the statement of pro/f.shortit and loss.
